nameStory: The "wrinkly" part is obvious once you see this fungus - its surface is deeply ridged and folded like a crumpled paper bag. The "stinkhorn" name comes from the family's notorious habit of producing foul-smelling spores that attract flies, and their often phallic shape that early botanists found too suggestive to ignore.
description: The Wrinkly Stinkhorn is a bizarre-looking fungus that emerges from an egg-like structure in the ground. When mature, it stands 3-5 inches tall with a deeply wrinkled, honeycomb-like cap that ranges from orange to reddish-brown. Like other stinkhorns, it produces a dark, smelly spore mass that flies love but humans definitely don't. The whole mushroom has an alien appearance that makes it unmistakable once you've seen one.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Produces an intensely foul odor like rotting meat or sewage that can be detected from several feet away, especially on warm days

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Deeply wrinkled and pitted surface resembling honeycomb or brain coral, colored orange to reddish-brown with dark spore slime in the crevices

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Hollow, white to pale yellow stem that feels spongy and fragile, often with a cup-like volva at the base

idTips.label: Egg Stage
idTips.description: Starts as a white to pinkish egg-shaped structure partially buried in soil or leaf litter, feeling firm but yielding to pressure

idTips.label: Spore Mass
idTips.description: Dark olive-green to black slimy coating in the wrinkles and pits, sticky to touch and intensely malodorous

habitat: Found in rich, moist soils in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, often near rotting logs or in areas with abundant organic matter. Prefers shaded locations with good moisture retention, particularly in oak-maple forests and woodland edges. Sometimes appears in mulched garden beds and compost-rich areas.

seasonality.spring: Egg stages may be present in late spring in warmer areas, buried in leaf litter and easily overlooked.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season from July through August, with mature specimens appearing after warm rains. The strong odor is most noticeable on hot, humid days.
seasonality.fall: Continues fruiting into early fall, especially during September's warm, wet periods. Late-season specimens may be less pungent but still identifiable by their wrinkled caps.
seasonality.winter: Not active during winter months, existing only as underground mycelium waiting for warmer conditions.

funFact: The putrid smell that makes humans gag is actually a sophisticated chemical advertisement - the fungus produces the same compounds found in rotting flesh to trick flies into thinking they've found the perfect place to lay eggs, ensuring the spores get spread far and wide on the insects' feet.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other stinkhorn species, but the deeply wrinkled, brain-like cap surface is distinctive. Remember: "Wrinkly cap, wrinkly name" - other stinkhorns have smoother caps or different shapes entirely.
contextualKnowledge: **SAFETY NOTE: Never eat wild mushrooms without expert identification. While not deadly poisonous, stinkhorns are generally considered inedible due to their revolting smell and taste.** Despite their off-putting nature, some cultures do consume young stinkhorn eggs before they develop their characteristic odor.
compareHints: Differs from its close relative Devil's Stinkhorn by having much deeper, more pronounced wrinkles and ridges on the cap surface, while Devil's Stinkhorn has a more netted or honeycomb pattern. The Wrinkly Stinkhorn also tends to be slightly smaller and has a more orange coloration compared to Devil's Stinkhorn's redder tones. Both smell equally terrible, so your nose won't help tell them apart!
